screens.title: Integrating Native Modules — Bridging JavaScript and Native Code
screens.subtitle: When JavaScript needs platform power: create, register, and call native code from React Native.

narration.text: In this lesson you'll learn why and how to extend React Native with native modules. Native modules let you write platform-specific code in Java, Kotlin, Objective‑C, or Swift and expose it to your JavaScript app. That ability matters when you need access to device features, optimized libraries, or platform APIs that JavaScript bindings don't yet provide. We'll walk through the bridge concept — the asynchronous messaging layer between the JavaScript thread and native threads — and show working examples for Android and iOS. You'll see how to define a native module, register it with React Native, and call it from JavaScript, including how to handle constants, callbacks, and promises. We'll also highlight common mistakes, such as blocking the main thread, forgetting to register a package, or failing to dispatch UI work on the main thread, and how to avoid them. By the end you'll be ready to implement a simple Toast or Alert native module and a CustomLogger that prints to native consoles, and you'll understand safety and testing practices that prevent crashes and leaks.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Native modules bridge JavaScript and platform code so you can access device features and optimized libraries while keeping UI responsive through asynchronous calls.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll build in this chapter

narration.text: These objectives map to practical skills you'll use when native code is required. First, you will identify situations where a native module is necessary — for example when a device A P I or highly optimized library is only available on the platform. Recognizing that need helps you make an informed design choice instead of hacking around missing features. Second, you'll understand the bridging mechanism: how asynchronous calls travel from JavaScript to native code and back. That understanding prevents a common mistake: treating native calls as synchronous. Third, you'll implement a simple Android native module, following the pattern of a Java class, a package that registers it, and adding that package to the application. Finally, you'll implement a simple iOS native module using the RCTBridgeModule protocol and RCT_EXPORT macros. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify that you can both explain and implement a working module on a device or emulator.

screens.title: When to use Native Modules
screens.subtitle: Deciding when platform code is necessary and why it matters

narration.text: Native modules are appropriate when JavaScript APIs and third-party libraries cannot provide the functionality or performance you need. For example, you may need access to a platform A P I that exposes hardware sensors, an existing optimized C++ library, or a UI element that must be implemented using native components. The decision matters because native modules add complexity: they require platform-specific code, additional build steps, and careful testing on devices. To choose correctly, ask whether a pure JavaScript solution would be significantly slower, or if the native A P I is only available on one platform. If so, a native module is justified. A common misconception is that native modules are inherently faster for every task; the reality is that they are best for platform-only features or heavy computations where native bindings already exist. When you implement native modules, prefer small, well-defined APIs that encapsulate platform work and return results asynchronously. That keeps your JavaScript logic simple and your UI responsive. Finally, plan for testing and error handling since native crashes affect the whole app. When to use Native Modules means use native modules for platform-only apis or heavy native libraries; avoid them for features already well-covered by javascript libraries.. In practical terms, deciding when platform code is necessary and why it matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Decision rule
keyIdea.text: Use native modules for platform-only APIs or heavy native libraries; avoid them for features already well-covered by JavaScript libraries.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › When to use Native Modules
When to use Native Modules
Deciding when platform code is necessary and why it matters
  • • Use them for device-only APIs, optimized native libraries, or platform UI not exposed to JS.
  • • Keep native APIs small and return results asynchronously to avoid blocking the UI.
  • • Test on device and handle errors carefully: native crashes affect the whole app.
  • • Avoid writing native code when a stable JS library already meets requirements.
Example
Integrate an optimized image-processing library that only exposes native bindings, and use a native module as a thin wrapper that accepts image paths and returns results via promises.
Analogy
Think of a native module as a short bridge connecting your JavaScript world to heavy machinery on the other side. Keep bridges simple and well-tested.
Takeaway
Reserve native modules for platform-only or performance-critical needs and design their API to be asynchronous and minimal.
Common mistake
Running heavy work on the main thread. Always move long-running tasks to background threads and resolve via callbacks or promises.

screens.title: How Bridging Works
screens.subtitle: The asynchronous messages that connect JS and native threads

narration.text: Bridging is the mechanism that lets JavaScript call native code and receive results without blocking the UI. Conceptually, JavaScript sends an asynchronous message over the bridge, which the native side receives and executes on its own thread. When execution completes, native code sends a result or triggers a callback back to JavaScript. Because communication is asynchronous, JavaScript continues to run while native work proceeds, keeping the UI responsive. A common error is assuming immediacy: calling a native method and immediately reading a result synchronously will fail. Instead, design your native methods to accept a callback or return a promise. Another important detail is thread context for UI updates: Android requires runOnUiThread and iOS requires dispatch_async on the main queue for UI operations. For long tasks, execute work on background threads in native code and resolve promises when finished. This pattern keeps the bridge predictable and avoids Application Not Responding errors or UI races. How Bridging Works means the bridge transmits asynchronous messages between javascript and native threads; design apis around callbacks or promises and respect main-thread rules for ui work.. In practical terms, the asynchronous messages that connect js and native threads. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Bridge principle
keyIdea.text: The bridge transmits asynchronous messages between JavaScript and native threads; design APIs around callbacks or promises and respect main-thread rules for UI work.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › How Bridging Works
Bridge process
Step-by-step flow that keeps the UI responsive
  1. JS sends async call: JavaScript invokes a native method via NativeModules.
  2. Bridge queues message: The call traverses the bridge as an asynchronous message.
  3. Native executes: Native code runs the requested work on an appropriate native thread.
  4. Return or event: Native resolves via callback, promise resolution, or emits an event back to JS.
Misconception
Assuming native calls are synchronous. Always treat them as asynchronous and design your code around callbacks or promises.
Threading rules
  • • Android UI changes must run on the main thread; use runOnUiThread.
  • • iOS UI updates must be dispatched to the main queue using dispatch_async(dispatch_get_main_queue(), ...).
  • • Long computations belong on background threads; return results with promises or callbacks.
Check your understanding
If a native method takes several seconds, how will you structure it so the UI does not freeze? Answer: perform work on a background thread and resolve a promise or callback when complete.

screens.title: Android Example — ToastModule.java
screens.subtitle: A minimal native module that shows a Toast and exports constants

narration.text: Let's walk through a concrete Android implementation pattern by examining a ToastModule. The module extends ReactContextBaseJavaModule, stores a ReactApplicationContext, and implements getName so JavaScript can reference it. Optional constants are provided through getConstants to expose values like SHORT and LONG durations. Methods intended for JavaScript must be marked with the ReactMethod annotation; in this example a show method accepts a message and a duration and calls the Android Toast A P I. Notice the logging call for debugging and that the Toast is created using getReactApplicationContext to obtain the native context. Important practical tips: ensure the package declaration matches your Android package name and add logging to help diagnose registration issues. After you create this class, register it via a ReactPackage so React Native knows about it. Remember that UI elements created from native code must be used on the main thread when required by the platform. Android Example — ToastModule.java means create a class extending reactcontextbasejavamodule, annotate methods with @reactmethod, and expose constants with getconstants.. In practical terms, a minimal native module that shows a toast and exports constants. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Android pattern
keyIdea.text: Create a class extending ReactContextBaseJavaModule, annotate methods with @ReactMethod, and expose constants with getConstants.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Android: ToastModule.java
ToastModule.java
A minimal module that exposes a show method and constants to JavaScript.
// android/app/src/main/java/com/yourprojectname/ToastModule.java
package com.yourprojectname; // Make sure this matches your package name

import com.facebook.react.bridge.NativeModule;
import com.facebook.react.bridge.ReactApplicationContext;
import com.facebook.react.bridge.ReactContext;
import com.facebook.react.bridge.ReactContextBaseJavaModule;
import com.facebook.react.bridge.ReactMethod;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.HashMap;

import android.widget.Toast;
import androidx.annotation.NonNull;
import android.util.Log; // For logging

public class ToastModule extends ReactContextBaseJavaModule {
    private static ReactApplicationContext reactContext;

    private static final String DURATION_SHORT_KEY = "SHORT";
    private static final String DURATION_LONG_KEY = "LONG";

    ToastModule(ReactApplicationContext context) {
        super(context);
        reactContext = context;
    }

    @NonNull
    @Override
    public String getName() {
        return "ToastExample"; // This is how you'll refer to the module in JS
    }

    @Override
    public Map getConstants() {
        final Map constants = new HashMap<>();
        constants.put(DURATION_SHORT_KEY, Toast.LENGTH_SHORT);
        constants.put(DURATION_LONG_KEY, Toast.LENGTH_LONG);
        return constants;
    }

    @ReactMethod
    public void show(String message, int duration) {
        Log.d("ToastModule", "Showing toast: " + message + " with duration: " + duration);
        Toast.makeText(getReactApplicationContext(), message, duration).show();
    }
}
Explanation
  • • getName tells React Native the module name that JS will use via NativeModules.ToastExample.
  • • getConstants exposes static values to JavaScript for convenience.
  • • Methods marked with @ReactMethod become callable from JavaScript and should be asynchronous in effect.
  • • Use logging to verify the module is registered and being called.
Concrete scenario
Use this module when you need a quick platform Toast for debug messages or transient user feedback that is best displayed in native form.
Key takeaway
Define a clear module name, expose only necessary methods, and return results asynchronously or via callbacks to keep the bridge predictable.

screens.title: Registering Your Android Module
screens.subtitle: Create a package and add it to MainApplication to make the module available to JS

narration.text: Creating the native class is only the first step. React Native needs to discover your module through a package. In Android, implement a ReactPackage that returns your module from createNativeModules and provide an empty list for createViewManagers unless you expose native views. After implementing MyAppPackage, you must add an instance of it to the packages list in MainApplication so the host loads it at runtime. A frequent error is forgetting to import or add the package, which leaves NativeModules. ToastExample undefined in JavaScript. Another common hiccup is mismatched package names — ensure your Java package lines match the project structure. When you update native code, rebuild the native app using the appropriate command. For development, use the platform build command to see native logs in Android Studio's Logcat. These steps complete the registration path from your Java class to JavaScript. Registering Your Android Module means add a reactpackage that returns your module and include it in mainapplication packages so react native loads it at startup.. In practical terms, create a package and add it to mainapplication to make the module available to js. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Registration path
keyIdea.text: Add a ReactPackage that returns your module and include it in MainApplication packages so React Native loads it at startup.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Registering Android Module
MyAppPackage.java
// android/app/src/main/java/com/yourprojectname/MyAppPackage.java
package com.yourprojectname;

import com.facebook.react.ReactPackage;
import com.facebook.react.bridge.NativeModule;
import com.facebook.react.bridge.ReactApplicationContext;
import com.facebook.react.uimanager.ViewManager;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.List;

public class MyAppPackage implements ReactPackage {

    @NonNull
    @Override
    public List createViewManagers(@NonNull ReactApplicationContext reactContext) {
        return Collections.emptyList();
    }

    @NonNull
    @Override
    public List createNativeModules(@NonNull ReactApplicationContext reactContext) {
        List modules = new ArrayList<>();
        modules.add(new ToastModule(reactContext)); // Add your module here
        return modules;
    }
}
Then add the package to MainApplication.java so the host loads it at startup and the module appears on NativeModules.
MainApplication changes
// In MainApplication.java add:
packages.add(new MyAppPackage()); // <-- Add your package here!
Debug tip
If NativeModules.YourModule is undefined, confirm the package is added and rebuild the native app. Check Android Studio Logcat for startup errors or package-not-found traces.
Takeaway
Registration ties your Java class to the RN host. Without it, JS cannot find or call the native module.

screens.title: iOS Example — ToastExample.h & .m
screens.subtitle: Export an Objective‑C module and present an alert on the main queue

narration.text: On iOS, native modules implement the RCTBridgeModule protocol. The header file declares the interface and the implementation file uses the RCT_EXPORT_MODULE macro to export the class to JavaScript. You can expose constants with constantsToExport and export methods with RCT_EXPORT_METHOD. In the ToastExample implementation, note the use of dispatch_async on the main queue before presenting a UIKit alert. UI work must occur on the main thread, and this pattern ensures the AlertController is presented safely. Logging through RCTLogInfo helps debug calls while developing in Xcode. A subtle but important point: if you have C++ or other native bindings, you may need Objective‑C++ files with an. mm extension or bridging headers. Finally, when you add these files in Xcode, ensure they are added to your app target so React Native can compile and load them. iOS Example — ToastExample.h & .m means implement rctbridgemodule, use rct_export_module and rct_export_method, and dispatch ui code to the main queue for safe ui updates.. In practical terms, export an objective‑c module and present an alert on the main queue. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: iOS pattern
keyIdea.text: Implement RCTBridgeModule, use RCT_EXPORT_MODULE and RCT_EXPORT_METHOD, and dispatch UI code to the main queue for safe UI updates.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › iOS: ToastExample
ToastExample.h
// ios/YourProjectName/ToastExample.h
#import <React/RCTBridgeModule.h>

@interface ToastExample : NSObject <RCTBridgeModule>
@end
ToastExample.m
// ios/YourProjectName/ToastExample.m
#import "ToastExample.h"
#import <React/RCTLog.h> // For logging to Xcode console
#import <UIKit/UIKit.h> // For UIAlertController

@implementation ToastExample

RCT_EXPORT_MODULE();

- (NSDictionary *)constantsToExport {
  return @{ @"DURATION_SHORT": @(0.5), @"DURATION_LONG": @(2.0) };
}

RCT_EXPORT_METHOD(show:(NSString*)message duration:(double)duration) {
  RCTLogInfo(@"Showing iOS Alert: %@ with duration: %f", message, duration);

  dispatch_async(dispatch_get_main_queue(), ^{
    UIAlertController *alert = [UIAlertController alertControllerWithTitle:@"React Native Alert"
                                                                   message:message
                                                            preferredStyle:UIAlertControllerStyleAlert];
    UIAlertAction *defaultAction = [UIAlertAction actionWithTitle:@"OK" style:UIAlertActionStyleDefault handler:^(UIAlertAction * action) {}];
    [alert addAction:defaultAction];

    UIViewController *rootViewController = [UIApplication sharedApplication].delegate.window.rootViewController;
    [rootViewController presentViewController:alert animated:YES completion:nil];

    if (duration > 0) {
      dispatch_after(dispatch_time(DISPATCH_TIME_NOW, (int64_t)(duration * NSEC_PER_SEC)), dispatch_get_main_queue(), ^{
        [alert dismissViewControllerAnimated:YES completion:nil];
      });
    }
  });
}

@end
Notes
  • • RCT_EXPORT_MODULE makes the Objective‑C class visible to JavaScript with its class name by default.
  • • Use constantsToExport to surface static values to JS.
  • • Always dispatch UI updates to the main queue using dispatch_async(dispatch_get_main_queue(), ...).
  • • If using C++ bindings, consider Objective‑C++ files and bridging headers as needed.
Concrete scenario: Use an iOS alert for immediate user feedback coming from native sensors or background services exposed by your module.
Takeaway
Export minimal, well-documented methods and ensure target membership in Xcode so the module is compiled into your app bundle.

screens.title: Calling Native Modules from JavaScript
screens.subtitle: Import NativeModules, access constants, call methods, and handle missing modules

narration.text: Calling native modules from React Native JavaScript is straightforward once the native side is registered. Import NativeModules from the framework and read the module by the name returned by getName or RCT_EXPORT_MODULE. You can access constants directly and invoke methods. Because native work is asynchronous, your JavaScript should check for the module's existence and handle absent modules gracefully, for example by showing an Alert when running in a pure web or managed environment that lacks native code. When a native method returns values, use promises and async/await or set up callbacks. For simple UI triggers like a Toast or Alert, call the exported show method directly and pass the appropriate duration constant depending on platform. During development, use platform-specific checks to ensure your code paths provide clear fallbacks. Testing on a device or emulator is required to see native UI elements and native console output. Calling Native Modules from JavaScript means use nativemodules.modulename to call exposed methods, check presence, and handle results via callbacks or promises.. In practical terms, import nativemodules, access constants, call methods, and handle missing modules. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Call pattern
keyIdea.text: Use NativeModules.ModuleName to call exposed methods, check presence, and handle results via callbacks or promises.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Calling from JavaScript
NativeModules usage example
import React from 'react';
import { Button, View, StyleSheet, NativeModules, Platform, Text, Alert } from 'react-native';

const ToastExample = NativeModules.ToastExample;

export default function NativeModuleComponent() {
  const showNativeToast = () => {
    if (ToastExample) {
      const duration = Platform.OS === 'android' ? ToastExample.SHORT : ToastExample.DURATION_SHORT;
      ToastExample.show('Hello from Native!', duration);
    } else {
      Alert.alert('Error', 'Native Toast module not found. Are you running on a device/emulator with native code?');
    }
  };

  return (
    
      Native Module Integration
      This triggers a platform-specific native UI element.
    
  );
}
Important patterns
  • • Check module presence: NativeModules.ModuleName may be undefined in non-native contexts.
  • • Choose constants by Platform.OS for platform-specific values.
  • • Use Alert or graceful fallback when native modules are unavailable.
  • • For returned results, prefer promises and async/await in JS.
Scenario: call show from a debug screen to confirm the native module is registered and observe Toast on Android or Alert on iOS.
Key takeaway
Always validate module availability and design JS to handle async native results; rebuild the app after native code changes.

screens.title: Handling Asynchronous Results: Callbacks, Promises, Events
screens.subtitle: Patterns for returning values and emitting events from native code

narration.text: Native modules can return results through callbacks, promises, or events. Callbacks are useful for simple, immediate responses where the native method invokes a provided function. Promises give a cleaner async/await pattern in JavaScript and are appropriate when native work may be longer running. For event-driven communication initiated from native code, use a NativeEventEmitter on the JavaScript side and send events from native. Choose the right pattern based on the interaction style: use promises for request-response, callbacks for lightweight responses, and events for continuous or unsolicited native signals. A frequent pitfall is failing to resolve or reject a promise on all code paths, which leaves the JavaScript caller waiting indefinitely. Always resolve or reject, and include robust error handling to avoid app instability. For long-running native operations, run work on background threads and return the result asynchronously to the bridge so the UI stays responsive. Handling Asynchronous Results: Callbacks, Promises, Events means use callbacks for quick responses, promises for clearer async flow, and events for unsolicited or streaming native signals; always handle errors and resolve promises.. In practical terms, patterns for returning values and emitting events from native code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Result patterns
keyIdea.text: Use callbacks for quick responses, promises for clearer async flow, and events for unsolicited or streaming native signals; always handle errors and resolve promises.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Async Results
Callbacks, Promises, and Events
Choose the pattern that fits the interaction style.
Callbacks: Pass a function from JS that native calls when work completes. Good for simple responses.
Promises: Native resolves or rejects a promise. Works well with async/await and longer operations.
Events: Use NativeEventEmitter to receive unsolicited updates from native code, such as sensor streams.
Pitfall: never leave a promise unresolved. Ensure every code path resolves or rejects to avoid hanging the JavaScript caller.
Practical tips
  • • For heavy work, schedule background threads and resolve promises afterward.
  • • Use events for continuous or push-style updates from native code.
  • • Add error payloads to rejections so JS can handle native errors gracefully.
Concrete example
If a native image processor takes time, run it on a background thread and return a promise that resolves with the processed image path when done.
Key takeaway
Select callbacks, promises, or events to match your interaction and always handle success and error paths explicitly.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Safety Notes
screens.subtitle: Avoid crashes, leaks, and ANRs by following platform rules

narration.text: Native code carries risks: a crash in native code will crash the whole app, and incorrect threading can cause UI freezes or races. Common mistakes include modifying UI from a background thread, forgetting to register the native package, mismatching package names or file targets, and failing to resolve promises. On Android, running long work on the main thread causes Application Not Responding errors. On iOS, UI must be updated on the main queue. Memory management is another concern, especially in Objective‑C: be mindful of object ownership and avoid leaks. Testing on device or emulator and watching native logs in Logcat or Xcode is essential to catch issues early. Use logging generously when developing native modules and add defensive error handling. The source stresses that native modules increase project complexity, so use them only when JavaScript solutions are insufficient and maintain robust tests and code reviews for native changes. Common Mistakes and Safety Notes means native code can crash your app. always handle threading, memory, and error paths carefully and test on real devices.. In practical terms, avoid crashes, leaks, and anrs by following platform rules. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Safety first
keyIdea.text: Native code can crash your app. Always handle threading, memory, and error paths carefully and test on real devices.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Common Mistakes & Safety
Common mistakes
  • • Running long computations on the main thread (Android ANR).
  • • Updating UI from a background thread instead of the main/UI thread.
  • • Forgetting to register the package or export the module macros.
  • • Leaving promises unresolved or not handling error paths.
Safety notes
  • • Crashes in native code crash your app; add robust error handling and tests.
  • • Watch memory management on iOS to avoid leaks in Objective‑C code.
  • • Check permissions and security when accessing sensitive device features.
  • • Test on real devices and monitor Logcat or Xcode console output during development.
Debugging checklist
Confirm package registration
Verify module name matches getName or RCT_EXPORT_MODULE
Rebuild native app after changes

screens.title: Activity — CustomLogger Native Module
screens.subtitle: Implement logMessage to write to Logcat and Xcode console and call it from JS

narration.text: This hands-on task guides you through implementing a CustomLogger native module that writes a message to the native console. On Android, create a CustomLoggerModule that extends ReactContextBaseJavaModule and implement logMessage using Android's Log. d with a custom tag. Add the module to your MyAppPackage and include it in MainApplication, then rebuild. package com.yourprojectname;

import com.facebook.react.bridge.ReactApplicationContext;
import com.facebook.react.bridge.ReactContextBaseJavaModule;
import com.facebook.react.bridge.ReactMethod;
import androidx.annotation.NonNull;
import android.util.Log;

public class CustomLoggerModule extends ReactContextBaseJavaModule {
    CustomLoggerModule(ReactApplicationContext context) {
        super(context);
    }

    @NonNull
    @Override
    public String getName() {
        return "CustomLogger";
    }

    @ReactMethod
    public void logMessage(String message) {
        Log.d("ReactNativeCustomLog", message);
    }
}

#import <React/RCTBridgeModule.h>

@interface CustomLogger : NSObject <RCTBridgeModule>
@end

#import "CustomLogger.h"
#import <React/RCTLog.h>

@implementation CustomLogger

RCT_EXPORT_MODULE();

RCT_EXPORT_METHOD(logMessage:(NSString*)message) {
  RCTLogInfo(@"ReactNativeCustomLog: %@", message);
}

@end

narration.text: Let's summarize the most important ideas from this chapter. First, native modules let you run platform-specific code from JavaScript, enabling access to device features or optimized libraries that the JavaScript ecosystem does not expose. Second, bridging is the asynchronous mechanism that sends messages between the JavaScript thread and native threads; respect its asynchronous nature and handle results via callbacks, promises, or events. Third, NativeModules is the JavaScript object you use to access exported native modules; always check for presence and provide graceful fallbacks. Remember these three concepts as the foundation: native modules for platform capability, the bridge for asynchronous communication, and NativeModules as the JS entry point. Keep your native APIs small, asynchronous, and well-tested to minimize risk. narration.text: A few technical reminders will help you avoid common pitfalls. On Android, extend ReactContextBaseJavaModule and mark callable methods with @ReactMethod. On iOS, conform to RCTBridgeModule and export methods with RCT_EXPORT_METHOD and classes with RCT_EXPORT_MODULE. Always ensure UI alterations occur on the platform's main thread using runOnUiThread on Android or dispatch_async to the main queue on iOS. When returning data, choose the right style: callbacks, promises, or events. Finally, remember that native code raises the bar for testing because a native crash affects the entire app, so keep native code minimal, add defensive checks, and validate behavior on real devices using Logcat and Xcode console diagnostics.
